blocks.text: The widow’s debt threatens more than the loss of property: her creditor is preparing to take her two sons as bondmen. Elisha’s instructions turn the family’s sole remaining resource—a pot of oil—into something that can be sold. The multiplying oil therefore answers the crisis in practical stages: the borrowed containers are filled, the oil is sold, the debt is paid, and the remaining proceeds support the widow and her sons.

The Shunammite woman’s relationship with Elisha begins with repeated hospitality. She provides food and then a dedicated room for the man of God; after Gehazi points out that she has no son and that her husband is old, Elisha promises her a child. When that promised child later dies, the narrative carefully traces her journey from Shunem to Elisha at Carmel. The response also unfolds in stages: Gehazi goes ahead with Elisha’s staff, but the child does not awaken; Elisha then arrives, prays to Jehovah, acts directly, and returns to the child before he opens his eyes.

The final scenes concern the prophetic community during famine. Food gathered for a shared stew becomes dangerous because unidentified wild gourds have been added, and the men’s cry that there is “death in the pot” brings the peril into the dialogue before Elisha makes the food harmless. Soon afterward, a man brings firstfruits and twenty barley loaves. Although the servant questions whether this can feed one hundred people, Elisha orders that it be distributed; the people eat and leave some over, exactly as the prophetic word had declared.

sections.title: Elisha Among Households and the Prophetic Community
